International trade is the exchange of goods and services across national borders, governed by differences in comparative advantage, factor endowments, and trade policies. A foundational topic in economics, it addresses why nations trade, who benefits, and how tariffs, quotas, and trade agreements shape commerce. David Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage, developed in the early nineteenth century, showed that nations gain from specializing in what they produce relatively cheaply, even if one is absolutely more productive. Countries export goods that use abundant factors of production intensively and import goods that use scarce factors intensively, a principle known as the Heckscher-Ohlin theorem. Trade barriers—including tariffs, quotas, and export subsidies—protect domestic producers from foreign competition but create deadweight loss, whereas free trade maximizes global efficiency. Comparative advantage explains why trade is mutually beneficial even when one country is more productive at everything. Both countries gain by specializing. Trade politics involves import-competing industries lobbying for protection while export industries advocate for open markets, and consumers benefit from lower prices. Modern trade is shaped by multilateral agreements like the GATT and WTO, regional trade blocs such as the EU and NAFTA, now called USMCA, and supply chains spanning multiple countries. These principles extend Adam Smith's earlier advocacy of free trade and his division of labor across national borders. Friedrich Hayek championed free trade against protectionism on efficiency grounds.
